sources_reopened.note: Abstract and full text match the record's passage, but the 79% any-use figure is one Discussion sentence, not a result (see issue on C11-P11).

Abstract confirms thresholds, consensus caveat and the conditional recommendations against pramipexole, ropinirole and rotigotine; 'normal iron results benefit' sentence is in the full-text Discussion (not re-opened).

sources_reopened.tool: PubMed get_article_metadata; get_full_text_article (empty body, no abstract)
sources_reopened.note: PubMed has no abstract and PMC body returned empty; the 22 of 25 and 74 to 347% figures could not be re-checked here and rest on the record's full-text passage.
FIREFLI tested falls and quality of life, not fires (see issue on C11-P04).

issues.text: For every 13 people who took a tablet, about 1 more reported better sleep than with a dummy pill (the true figure could be anywhere from about 7 to 63).
issues.problem: NNT of 13 comes from only 4 of the 24 trials (1,072 people) testing zaleplon, brotizolam, nitrazepam or loprazolam, with the outcome 'improved sleep quality'; the range is a 95% confidence interval, not 'anywhere'. Population of this figure is narrower than the sentence implies.
issues.source_says: 'On the basis of four studies (1072 participants), the number of patients who would need to be treated with a sedative (zaleplon, brotizolam or nitrazepam, or loprazolam) for one to have an improvement in sleep quality is 13 (95% CI 6.7 to 62.9).'
issues.replacement: In 4 of the trials (1,072 people, testing zaleplon, brotizolam, nitrazepam or loprazolam), for every 13 people who took a tablet, about 1 more rated their sleep quality as improved than with a dummy pill (95% confidence range about 7 to 63).

issues.text: For every 6 people who took one, about 1 more had a side effect.
issues.problem: Harm figure (NNH) given without the matching benefit figure (NNT 13) or the authors' 'rough guide only' caveat and the fact that the two come from different trials; unbalanced in a 'Weighing it up' post and drops a required qualification.
issues.source_says: Authors: the NNT:NNH ratio 'can be used as a rough indicator only'; NNT from 4 trials, NNH (any adverse event) from 16 trials.
issues.replacement: For every 6 people who took one, about 1 more had a side effect of any kind (a rough guide, from different trials than the sleep figures).

issues.text: Among 1,280 people with sleep-study confirmed disease in 24 specialist centres, about 6 in 100 a year went on to develop Parkinson's disease, dementia with Lewy bodies or a related condition.
issues.problem: 'Confirmed disease' is vague and omits that participants had no parkinsonism or dementia at the start, which is what makes 'went on to develop' valid.
issues.source_says: 'patients with polysomnographically-confirmed iRBD without parkinsonism or dementia' at baseline; 6.3% a year; outcome Parkinson's disease, dementia with Lewy bodies or multiple system atrophy.
issues.replacement: Among 1,280 people in 24 specialist centres whose REM sleep behaviour disorder was confirmed by a sleep study and who did not yet have Parkinson's disease or dementia, about 6 in 100 a year went on to develop Parkinson's disease, dementia with Lewy bodies or a related condition.

issues.text: In 1,280 people with sleep-study confirmed disease in 24 specialist centres, about 6 in 100 a year went on to develop Parkinson's disease, dementia with Lewy bodies or a related condition, and the estimate by 12 years was about 3 in 4.
issues.problem: Same vagueness as X: baseline absence of parkinsonism/dementia not stated; the 12-year figure is a Kaplan-Meier estimate with average follow-up of only 4.6 years.
issues.source_says: Average follow-up 4.6 years (range 1-19); 'with 73.5% converting after 12-year follow-up' (Kaplan-Meier).
issues.replacement: In 1,280 people in 24 specialist centres whose REM sleep behaviour disorder was confirmed by a sleep study and who had no Parkinson's disease or dementia at the start, about 6 in 100 a year went on to develop Parkinson's disease, dementia with Lewy bodies or a related condition, and the estimated figure by 12 years was about 3 in 4 (average follow-up was 4.6 years).

issues.text: In one specialist cohort, people whose symptoms came with antidepressants still showed early signs of Parkinson-type disease, so a medicines review should not end the assessment.
issues.problem: Omits the same cohort's finding that antidepressant-associated cases had a LOWER 5-year risk of neurodegenerative disease than other cases (but not zero); 'early signs of Parkinson-type disease' is looser than 'abnormalities on tests of neurodegeneration'. Reads as more alarming than the source.
issues.source_says: Postuma 2013 (per claim record C11-21-e): 12/14 neurodegenerative markers abnormal vs controls, but 5-year risk of developing neurodegenerative disease 22% vs 59% (RR 0.22) compared with those not on antidepressants; small single-centre cohort of 100.
issues.replacement: In one small specialist cohort, people whose symptoms came with antidepressants still had abnormalities on tests of nerve-cell loss, although their five-year risk of going on to develop Parkinson's disease or dementia was lower than in people without antidepressants (22 in 100 against 59 in 100). So a medicines review should not end the assessment.

issues.text: Mailing information alone did not reduce use in a large US trial in people with dementia.
issues.problem: Does not say use of what. The US trial targeted antipsychotics, sedative-hypnotics and strong anticholinergics (not benzodiazepines specifically) and mailed to both patient and prescriber; in context a reader will assume benzodiazepine use.
issues.source_says: Singh 2024: 12,787 people with Alzheimer's disease/related dementias; mailing to patient and prescriber; 76.7% vs 77.5% still dispensed a targeted high-risk medication at 6 months.
issues.replacement: Mailing information to people with dementia and their prescribers did not reduce use of high-risk medicines, including sedatives, in a large US trial.

issues.text: Mailing information alone did not reduce use in a large US trial in people with dementia
issues.problem: Same missing object ('use' of what) on the visual and alt text.
issues.source_says: As above.
issues.replacement: Mailing information did not reduce use of high-risk medicines (including sedatives) in a large US trial in people with dementia

issues.text: A second Quebec trial, in which pharmacists sent a brochure to patients and a recommendation to stop to their doctors,
issues.problem: In D-PRESCRIBE pharmacists were 'encouraged to send' the brochure; 'sent' overstates delivery. Also 'the researchers say the results need testing elsewhere' (later in the caption) is a statement from the D-PRESCRIBE authors only; the EMPOWER abstract makes no such statement.
issues.source_says: 'Pharmacists in the intervention group were encouraged to send patients an educational deprescribing brochure in parallel to sending their physicians an evidence-based pharmaceutical opinion to recommend deprescribing.' 'The generalizability of these findings to other settings requires further research.' (D-PRESCRIBE only)
issues.replacement: A second Quebec trial, in which pharmacists were encouraged to send patients a brochure and to send their doctors a recommendation to stop,

issues.text: were more likely to have stopped at 6 months: 27 in 100 against 5 in 100 with usual care.
issues.problem: 'Stopped' is not defined; it means no further pharmacy refills, not confirmed abstinence. The definition is needed because the whole result depends on it.
issues.source_says: 'Benzodiazepine therapy discontinuation at 6 months ... ascertained by pharmacy medication renewal profiles.'
issues.replacement: were more likely to have stopped refilling at 6 months: 27 in 100 against 5 in 100 with usual care.

issues.text: Whether the visits themselves reduce fires or injuries is unproven. A trial that set out to test it recruited 63 of a planned 1,156 people and concluded the evidence remains inconclusive.
issues.problem: FIREFLI did not test fires. Its primary outcomes were falls and quality of life in people aged 65 and over; it recruited 63 of 1,156 and could not do its planned analyses. Describing it as testing 'fires or injuries' misstates the study.
issues.source_says: FIREFLI RCT: primary outcomes number of falls and EQ-5D-5L over 12 months; 63 randomised; 'the planned statistical and health economic analyses could not be conducted'; 'The evidence for the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of Home Fire Safety Visits remains inconclusive.'
issues.replacement: Whether the visits themselves reduce falls or improve quality of life in older people is unproven. A trial that set out to test this recruited only 63 of a planned 1,156 people and could not run its planned analyses; its authors concluded the evidence remains inconclusive. No trial evidence on fires was found.

issues.text: The study was small: 38 adults aged 18 to 80, so not only older people, tested in deep sleep only.
issues.problem: Hearing-loss severity is missing in X, Bluesky, Threads, the visual and alt text (headline sentences say 'adults with hearing loss'). Participants had mild to moderately severe loss (25 to 70 dB); results may not apply to profound loss.
issues.source_says: '38 adults (aged 18 to 80 yr) with mild to moderately severe hearing loss of 25 to 70 dB (in both ears), during slow-wave sleep'.
issues.replacement: The study was small: 38 adults aged 18 to 80 with mild to moderately severe hearing loss, so not only older people, tested in deep sleep only.

issues.text: Out of 100 adults with hearing loss in deep sleep, in a laboratory.
issues.problem: Same missing severity qualifier on the chart slide and alt text; the chart's second line also omits it.
issues.source_says: Mild to moderately severe hearing loss, 25 to 70 dB.
issues.replacement: Out of 100 adults with mild to moderately severe hearing loss in deep sleep, in a laboratory.

issues.text: If you sleep without hearing aids, ask your fire service about a pad alarm.
issues.problem: Drops the key qualification (kept in X and LinkedIn) that the report does not say whether hearing aids were worn; also the pad-alarm availability is only a question to ask (search-extract support).
issues.source_says: Abstract does not state hearing aid use; C11-13-d partly supported: phrase only as a question.
issues.replacement: The study did not say whether hearing aids were worn. If you sleep without them, ask your fire and rescue service whether they can fit an alarm with a vibrating pad.

issues.text: The pads were commercial products as sold in 2009.
issues.problem: 'As sold in 2009' is not stated; the abstract says shakers were tested at the intensity 'as purchased'.
issues.source_says: 'Bed and pillow shakers awoke 80 to 84% at the intensity level as purchased.' Published 2009.
issues.replacement: The pads were commercial products tested at the intensity as purchased, and the study was published in 2009.

issues.text: In older adults, brief behavioural treatment beat printed information, 2 in 3 against 1 in 4.
issues.problem: A single small single-centre trial (79 people) is written as a general finding in older adults; no sample size, timeframe or 'small' qualifier. The claim record requires 'small single-centre trial, primary outcome at 4 weeks'.
issues.source_says: Buysse 2011: 79 older adults (mean age 71.7), response 67% vs 25% at 4 weeks, maintained at 6 months; one US centre.
issues.replacement: In a small US trial of 79 older adults, brief behavioural treatment beat printed information at 4 weeks: about 2 in 3 responded against 1 in 4.

issues.text: In 79 older adults (average age 72), about 2 in 3 improved after two nurse sessions and two phone calls of behavioural treatment, against 1 in 4 given printed information.
issues.problem: Missing 'small US trial' and the 4-week timeframe of the primary outcome ('improved' = a defined treatment response).
issues.source_says: 'Categorically defined response (67% vs 25%)' at 4 weeks; improvements maintained at 6 months.
issues.replacement: In a small US trial of 79 older adults (average age 72), about 2 in 3 had responded at 4 weeks after two nurse sessions and two phone calls of behavioural treatment, against 1 in 4 given printed information.

issues.text: A 2025 US guideline (AASM) suggests iron if ferritin is 75 or below, even when a result looks normal, and advises against pramipexole and ropinirole as standard.
issues.problem: Drops the required qualification that the iron cut-offs are expert consensus that has not been tested directly (carried in X, LinkedIn, Threads and the visual) and that the advice against dopamine agonists is conditional. 'Even when a result looks normal' states the cut-off as established.
issues.source_says: 'Consensus guidelines, which have not been empirically tested, suggest ... iron ... if serum ferritin <= 75 ng/mL or transferrin saturation < 20%'; pramipexole, ropinirole, rotigotine: 'suggests against the standard use' (conditional).
issues.replacement: Restless legs in an older person: check ferritin and the medicines list first. A 2025 US guideline (AASM) suggests iron if ferritin is 75 or below (untested expert consensus), even when the result looks normal. It conditionally advises against pramipexole and ropinirole as standard. Weigh gabapentinoid sleepiness and dizziness.

issues.text: It puts gabapentin and pregabalin first among medicines.
issues.problem: The guideline ranks recommendations by strength within PICO groups; it does not designate gabapentinoids 'first' among medicines (IV ferric carboxymaltose is also a strong recommendation and gabapentin enacarbil is listed before gabapentin). Same wording in LinkedIn ('now puts ... first among medicines').
issues.source_says: 'The AASM recommends the use of gabapentin enacarbil / gabapentin / pregabalin (strong recommendation, moderate certainty)'; also strong for IV ferric carboxymaltose.
issues.replacement: It strongly recommends gabapentin and pregabalin (and, with appropriate iron status, intravenous iron).

issues.text: Why dopamine agonists are no longer standard: augmentation
issues.problem: Presents a conditional guideline suggestion as a settled change in standard practice and drops the AASM attribution on this line; same in alt text ('dopamine agonists no longer standard').
issues.source_says: 'AASM suggests against the standard use of pramipexole/ropinirole/rotigotine (conditional recommendation)'; dopamine agonists remain effective short term.
issues.replacement: Why the guideline advises against dopamine agonists as standard treatment: augmentation (conditional recommendation)

issues.text: Sleep itself improved only modestly: sustained insomnia remission was 26% with CBT and 19% with sleep education.
issues.problem: Interpretation not in the source. The outcome is continuous remission throughout follow-up (a strict outcome); a low rate does not show that sleep 'improved only modestly'.
issues.source_says: 'Remission of insomnia disorder continuously sustained before depression event or during follow-up was more likely in CBT-I participants (41 [26.3%]) compared with the SET participants (26 [19.3%], P = .03).'
issues.replacement: Insomnia remission that lasted through follow-up was uncommon in both groups: 26% with CBT and 19% with sleep education.

issues.text: Their guidance says hospitals should either have a machine available or ask patients to bring their own.
issues.problem: The recommendation is 'we suggest that facilities should consider having PAP equipment available or have the patient bring their own'; 'should either ... or' reads firmer. Same wording in LinkedIn.
issues.source_says: Recommendation 3.1.3: 'Facilities Should Consider Having PAP Equipment for Perioperative Use Available or Have the Patient Bring Their Own'; 'Local institutional policies may determine how this matter is to be handled'.
issues.replacement: Their guidance suggests hospitals should consider either having a machine available or asking patients to bring their own.

issues.text: A second SASM guideline covers drugs given during and after surgery. It says strong painkillers such as morphine-type drugs, and some sedatives, may make breathing problems more likely in people with sleep apnoea. The evidence for this is limited, so it is graded as a weak recommendation.
issues.problem: The second guideline is on intraoperative management, not 'during and after surgery'. The sedative statement is for intravenous benzodiazepine sedation, whose evidence is graded moderate (recommendation weak); only the opioid statement is low-evidence.
issues.source_says: Memtsoudis 2018 'Guideline on Intraoperative Management': opioids - level of evidence low, grade weak; IV benzodiazepine sedation - level of evidence moderate, grade weak.
issues.replacement: A second SASM guideline, on care during surgery, says strong painkillers such as morphine-type drugs, and intravenous sedatives of the benzodiazepine type, may make breathing problems more likely in people with sleep apnoea. The recommendations are graded weak, and the evidence for the painkiller statement is graded low.

issues.text: Anaesthesia and sleep specialists advise keeping it up around an operation.
issues.problem: Drops the scope (guidance is for planned/surgical admissions), which X and the visual state; Threads then adds the unexpected-admission advice without saying it goes beyond the guidance.
issues.source_says: SASM 2016 guideline is on perioperative care of adults having surgery; extending to unplanned admissions is a practical suggestion only.
issues.replacement: Anaesthesia and sleep specialists advise keeping it up around a planned operation.

issues.text: In other sleep problems the average gain was about 7 minutes quicker to sleep.
issues.problem: Omits that the meta-analysis pooled adults AND children with primary sleep disorders and was not specific to older people (stated in X and LinkedIn). Population swap risk in a post about older people.
issues.source_says: Ferracioli-Oda 2013: 'Adults and children diagnosed with primary sleep disorders'; WMD 7.06 min sleep latency, 8.25 min total sleep time.
issues.replacement: In adults and children together with other sleep problems, the average gain was about 7 minutes quicker to sleep.

issues.text: In other people with sleep problems the average gain was about 7 minutes quicker to sleep and 8 minutes more of it.
issues.problem: Same omission: pooled adults and children, not older people.
issues.source_says: As above.
issues.replacement: In adults and children together with insomnia and other sleep problems, the average gain was about 7 minutes quicker to sleep and 8 minutes more of it.

issues.text: Other sleep problems: about 7 minutes quicker to sleep, about 8 minutes more sleep, on average
issues.problem: Same omission on the visual and alt text; the data label in the brief says 'mixed ages' but the printed text does not.
issues.source_says: As above.
issues.replacement: Other sleep problems (adults and children together): about 7 minutes quicker to sleep, about 8 minutes more sleep, on average

issues.text: in other sleep problems about 7 minutes quicker to sleep and 8 minutes more sleep on average
issues.problem: Same omission in the alt text.
issues.source_says: As above.
issues.replacement: in other sleep problems, in adults and children together, about 7 minutes quicker to sleep and 8 minutes more sleep on average

issues.text: For total night-time sleep the difference was about 11 minutes, and the range ran from 16 minutes less to 38 minutes more.
issues.problem: Direction not stated (about 11 minutes more with melatonin) and it rests on only 2 of the trials (184 people).
issues.source_says: 'total nocturnal sleep time (MD 10.68 minutes, 95% CI -16.22 to 37.59; 2 studies, n = 184)'.
issues.replacement: For total night-time sleep, melatonin gave about 11 minutes more (from two small trials of 184 people), and the range ran from 16 minutes less to 38 minutes more.

issues.text: In another US study, residents' night-time waking was linked with noise and changes in light. Cutting noise and light reduced the waking linked to light, but on its own did not improve most measures of sleep.
issues.problem: First sentence is the paper's introduction/background, not a finding of the study (the claim record warns of this). Also the intervention was multicomponent (staff feedback, noise abatement and individualised night continence care), so 'on its own' is not accurate.
issues.source_says: Schnelle 1999: background 'The sleep of nursing home residents is fragmented ... associated, at least in part, with environmental variables'; result: intervention improved only awakenings associated with light and with noise plus light; 'did not lead to significant improvements in the day sleep and most night sleep measures'.
issues.replacement: In another US trial (267 residents with incontinence in eight nursing homes), staff feedback on noise, noise abatement and less disruptive night continence care reduced noise and light changes. It reduced awakenings linked with light, and with noise plus light, but did not improve most other measures of sleep.

issues.text: Small US studies: checks set by skin risk cut waking with no skin harm.
issues.problem: Overgeneralised: the intervention reduced care-related waking (awakenings due to light and sound from continence care), not waking overall.
issues.source_says: 'Awakenings due to light and sound associated with incontinence care were significantly reduced ... no adverse changes in skin health or on most risk factors associated with skin.'
issues.replacement: Small US studies in residents with incontinence: checks set by skin risk cut care-related waking with no skin harm.

issues.text: In small US studies, checks set by each person's skin risk cut care-related waking with no harm to skin.
issues.problem: Population omitted: residents with incontinence. Also, 'no harm to skin' is over the short study period only.
issues.source_says: Participants were incontinent nursing home residents; authors recommend evaluating long-term effects on skin health.
issues.replacement: In small US studies of residents with incontinence, checks set by each person's skin risk cut care-related waking with no adverse change in skin health over the study period.

issues.text: In US nursing home studies, a wet episode was linked with about 4 in 100 night-time awakenings, while the light and noise of routine checks were linked with waking.
issues.problem: Population omitted (residents with incontinence), and the second clause rests on the Schnelle 1998 abstract's background sentence about a previous study rather than a measured result of that trial (its measured result was that awakenings due to light and sound from care fell). The Ouslander authors also caution about sensor limits.
issues.source_says: Ouslander 1998: 73 incontinent residents in three homes; 'Only 4% of the awakenings were associated with an incontinence episode'; 'Our findings must be interpreted cautiously because of limitations in the technologies and definitions we used'.
issues.replacement: In US nursing home studies of residents with incontinence, a wet episode was linked with about 4 in 100 night-time awakenings, and awakenings caused by the light and noise of continence care fell when care was individualised.

issues.text: In interviews, UK care home staff say there are too few night staff to help residents who wake.
issues.problem: Generalises 18 staff in four care homes, all talking about residents with dementia, to 'UK care home staff'.
issues.source_says: Webster 2022: 18 nurses and care assistants in four UK care homes, residents living with dementia; 'insufficient staffing at night'.
issues.replacement: In interviews in four UK care homes, staff caring for residents with dementia said there are too few night staff to help residents who wake.

issues.text: about 4 in 100 night-time awakenings were linked with a wet episode.
issues.problem: Authors' measurement caveat omitted: sleep, awakenings and wetness were detected by actigraphy and wired pads and the authors say findings must be interpreted cautiously; 73 residents, three homes.
issues.source_says: 'Our findings must be interpreted cautiously because of limitations in the technologies and definitions we used to identify sleep, awakenings, and incontinence.'
issues.replacement: about 4 in 100 night-time awakenings were linked with a wet episode (73 residents in three homes; the authors caution that the sleep and wetness sensors had limits).

issues.text: In England in 2020, about 1 in 5 people aged 60 and over living at home did not use the internet.
issues.problem: The 1-in-5 figure (79% used the internet at any frequency, aged 60+) is a single passing sentence in the Discussion ('comparable ELSA estimates ... suggest ... 79%'), used to contrast with China; it is not a reported result, there is no table or method for it. The Results report only daily use in adults 50+ (73.9% in June/July 2020). It is used as a visual headline stat (twenty-person icon grid, '1 in 5 did not use the internet'). Appears in X, LinkedIn, Bluesky, Threads, visual slide 2 and alt text.
issues.source_says: Discussion: 'comparable ELSA estimates (i.e., proportion of users of any frequency, aged 60 +) suggest that in England, this remained constant at 79% before and during the pandemic.' Results: daily internet use among adults 50+ 71.8% (2018/19) and 73.9% (June/July 2020); care home residents excluded and non-users may be under-represented.
issues.replacement: In a national study of people living at home in England, the authors' estimate was that about 79 in 100 people aged 60 and over used the internet at all in 2020, so about 1 in 5 did not. (Visual: 'about 1 in 5 did not use the internet, as estimated in a national study of people living at home.' Prefer the Results figure if the claim needs a firm number: daily use among adults aged 50 and over was 74 in 100 in 2020, so about 1 in 4 did not use the internet daily.)

issues.text: CBT for insomnia by phone helped older adults in a US trial: a year later 56 in 100 had no significant insomnia against 26 in 100 given information.
issues.problem: Omits that every participant had osteoarthritis pain, and that the 56 and 26 in 100 are among those followed up (119 and 128 of 327). 'Older adults' reads as all older adults with insomnia.
issues.source_says: 327 people aged 60+ with insomnia and osteoarthritis pain; 12-month remission 67 of 119 (56.3%) vs 33 of 128 (25.8%) among those with follow-up data.
issues.replacement: CBT for insomnia by phone helped older adults with insomnia and osteoarthritis pain in a US trial: a year later, among those followed up, 56 in 100 had no clinically significant insomnia against 26 in 100 given information.

issues.text: In a US trial of 327 people aged 60 and over, a year later 56 in 100 of those followed up had no significant insomnia, against 26 in 100 given information.
issues.problem: Omits that all 327 had osteoarthritis pain (included in X and LinkedIn).
issues.source_says: Participants 60+ with moderate to severe insomnia and osteoarthritis pain, one US health plan.
issues.replacement: In a US trial of 327 people aged 60 and over with insomnia and osteoarthritis pain, a year later 56 in 100 of those followed up had no clinically significant insomnia, against 26 in 100 given information.

issues.text: In a US trial of 327 people aged 60 and over with insomnia and arthritis pain,
issues.problem: The condition was osteoarthritis pain specifically (LinkedIn and the visual alt text use it for the trial, X says 'arthritis').
issues.source_says: 'older adults with moderate to severe osteoarthritis pain'.
issues.replacement: In a US trial of 327 people aged 60 and over with insomnia and osteoarthritis pain,

issues.text: is the first treatment recommended for long-term insomnia in US guidelines from the American College of Physicians and the American Academy of Sleep Medicine.
issues.problem: ACP calls CBT-I the initial treatment; the AASM behavioural guideline strongly recommends multicomponent CBT-I but does not rank it above medicines (its scope is behavioural treatments).
issues.source_says: ACP: 'initial treatment for chronic insomnia disorder'. AASM 2021: 'We recommend that clinicians use multicomponent CBT-I for the treatment of chronic insomnia disorder in adults (STRONG).'
issues.replacement: is the initial treatment recommended for long-term insomnia by the American College of Physicians, and is strongly recommended by the American Academy of Sleep Medicine.

issues.text: A sedative adds about 25 minutes of self-reported sleep in people over 60, with more confusion and daytime tiredness.
issues.problem: Visual body presents the trial average as what 'a sedative' adds, with no 'in trials', 'on average' or nightly-use qualifier. The post is about a single as-required dose on a ward, which these trials did not test (the caption says so). Same text in alt text.
issues.source_says: Glass 2005: trials of at least 5 consecutive nights (5 nights to 9 weeks) of any sedative hypnotic vs placebo in people aged 60+; mean 25.2 minutes; odds of cognitive and daytime fatigue events higher.
issues.replacement: In trials of sleeping tablets taken for at least 5 nights, people over 60 reported about 25 more minutes of sleep on average, with more confusion and daytime tiredness.

issues.text: In people over 60, tablets added about 25 minutes of sleep with more confusion.
issues.problem: Drops 'self-reported', 'on average', 'in trials of at least 5 nights' and 'daytime tiredness'; the not-a-single-dose qualification is the point of the post.
issues.source_says: As above.
issues.replacement: In trials of at least 5 nights in people over 60, sleeping tablets added about 25 minutes of self-reported sleep on average, with more confusion and daytime tiredness.

issues.text: In people over 60, tablets added only about 25 minutes of self-reported sleep, with more confusion and daytime tiredness.
issues.problem: Drops 'in trials of at least 5 nights' / 'on average'; reads as applying to one dose on a ward.
issues.source_says: As above.
issues.replacement: In trials of at least 5 nights in people over 60, tablets added only about 25 minutes of self-reported sleep on average, with more confusion and daytime tiredness.

issues.text: Tonight's call is pain, a full bladder and noise.
issues.problem: The survey reported 'toilet visits', not a full bladder, as a disturber, and reported disturbers rather than causes in any one patient.
issues.source_says: 'The most reported sleep-disturbing factors were noise of other patients, medical devices, pain, and toilet visits.'
issues.replacement: Tonight's call is to ask about pain, needing the toilet, noise and equipment.

issues.text: In a survey of 2,005 patients in 39 Dutch hospitals (median age 68), people reported sleeping 83 minutes less than at home.
issues.problem: X omits that the survey covered all adult ages, one night, self-reported (LinkedIn has it); the post is about older patients.
issues.source_says: Single-day survey, 22 February 2017, adults 18+ able to consent; 83 minutes shorter (95% CI 75-92).
issues.replacement: In a one-night survey of 2,005 adult patients of all ages in 39 Dutch hospitals (median age 68), people reported sleeping 83 minutes less than at home.
